sn47.13:1.1.pli: Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
sn47.13:1.1.eng: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
sn47.13:1.1.comm: This event follows SN 47.12 at Nāḷandā and precedes SN 47.14 at Ukkacelā on the Vajjian shore of the Ganges, so the Buddha must have been somewhere on the road between them, not in Sāvatthī. The commentary rather implausibly tries to reconcile this by proposing that the eighty-year old Buddha and Sāriputta took a side journey of over a thousand kilometres. It is simpler to assume that, since Sāvatthī was the default location for teachings and is often ascribed as a matter of convention, it was mentioned here by mistake.

sn47.13:1.2.pli: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā sāriputto magadhesu viharati nālakagāmake ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno.
sn47.13:1.2.eng: At that time Venerable Sāriputta was staying in the Magadhan lands near the little village of Nālaka, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn47.13:1.3.pli: Cundo ca samaṇuddeso āyasmato sāriputtassa upaṭṭhāko hoti.
sn47.13:1.3.eng: And the novice Cunda was his carer.
sn47.13:1.3.comm: The commentaries identify “novice Cunda”, who reported the deaths of Sāriputta (SN 47.13:1.3) and Mahāvīra (DN 29:2.1, MN 104:3.1), as Sāriputta’s younger brother, explaining that the title “novice” was a nickname that persisted from the time he ordained as a young novice. The commentaries further identify him with Mahācunda, one of the great disciples (MN 118:, AN 6.17, MN 8), who later brought the Dhamma to the land of the Cetīs (AN 6.46, AN 10.24), and once stayed with Channa and Sāriputta (MN 144:4.1, SN 35.87:1.2).

sn47.13:2.1.pli: Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto teneva ābādhena parinibbāyi.
sn47.13:2.1.eng: Then Venerable Sāriputta was fully extinguished from that sickness.

sn47.13:2.2.pli: Atha kho cundo samaṇuddeso āyasmato sāriputtassa pattacīvaramādāya yena sāvatthi jetavanaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmo yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho cundo samaṇuddeso āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca:
sn47.13:2.2.eng: Then Cunda took Sāriputta’s bowl and robes and set out for Sāvatthī. He went to see Venerable Ānanda at Jeta’s grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:
sn47.13:2.2.comm: Sāriputta’s passing is treated with simplicity and dignity. There is no mention of relics, or any supernatural occurrences.

sn47.13:2.3.eng: “Sir, Venerable Sāriputta has become fully quenched.

sn47.13:2.4.eng: This is his bowl and robe.”

sn47.13:3.1.pli: “Atthi kho idaṃ, āvuso cunda, kathāpābhataṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya.
sn47.13:3.1.eng: “Reverend Cunda, we should see the Buddha about this matter.

sn47.13:3.2.pli: Āyāmāvuso cunda, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamissāma; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocessāmā”ti.
sn47.13:3.2.eng: Come, let’s go to the Buddha and inform him about this.”

sn47.13:3.3.pli: “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho cundo samaṇuddeso āyasmato ānandassa paccassosi.

sn47.13:4.1.pli: Atha kho āyasmā ca ānando cundo ca samaṇuddeso yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca:
sn47.13:4.1.eng: Then Ānanda and Cunda went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn47.13:4.3.eng: Venerable Sāriputta has become fully quenched.

sn47.13:4.4.eng: This is his bowl and robe.

sn47.13:4.5.pli: Api ca me, bhante, madhurakajāto viya kāyo, disāpi me na pakkhāyanti, dhammāpi maṃ nappaṭibhanti ‘āyasmā sāriputto parinibbuto’ti sutvā”.
sn47.13:4.5.eng: Since I heard this, my body feels like it’s drugged. I’m disorientated, and the teachings don’t spring to mind.”

sn47.13:5.1.pli: “Kiṃ nu kho te, ānanda, sāriputto sīlakkhandhaṃ vā ādāya parinibbuto, samādhikkhandhaṃ vā ādāya parinibbuto, paññākkhandhaṃ vā ādāya parinibbuto, vimuttikkhandhaṃ vā ādāya parinibbuto, vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhaṃ vā ādāya parinibbuto”ti?
sn47.13:5.1.eng: “Well, Ānanda, when Sāriputta was fully quenched, did he take away your entire spectrum of ethical conduct, of immersion, of wisdom, of freedom, or of the knowledge and vision of freedom?”
sn47.13:5.1.comm: These five “spectrums” (dhammakkhandha) are normally said to be the qualities of arahants (SN 3.24:3.6, AN 10.12:2.2). This is anomalous, as Ānanda is still a trainee and has not fully developed the last two. See also SN 55.26:17.1, where the stream-enterer Anāthapiṇḍika is said to possess right knowledge and right freedom.

sn47.13:5.2.pli: “Na ca kho me, bhante, āyasmā sāriputto sīlakkhandhaṃ vā ādāya parinibbuto, samādhikkhandhaṃ vā …pe…

sn47.13:5.6.pli: Api ca me, bhante, āyasmā sāriputto ovādako ahosi otiṇṇo viññāpako sandassako samādapako samuttejako sampahaṃsako, akilāsu dhammadesanāya, anuggāhako sabrahmacārīnaṃ.
sn47.13:5.6.eng: But Venerable Sāriputta was my adviser and counselor. He educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired me. He never tired of teaching the Dhamma, and he supported his spiritual companions.
sn47.13:5.6.comm: Text’s otiṇṇo appears to be an error and I ignore it.

sn47.13:5.7.pli: Taṃ mayaṃ āyasmato sāriputtassa dhammojaṃ dhammabhogaṃ dhammānuggahaṃ anussarāmā”ti.
sn47.13:5.7.eng: I remember the nectar of the teaching, the riches of the teaching, the support of the teaching given by Venerable Sāriputta.”

sn47.13:6.1.eng: “Ānanda, did I not prepare for this when I explained that

sn47.13:6.2.eng: we must be parted and separated from all we hold dear and beloved?

sn47.13:6.3.pli: Taṃ kutettha, ānanda, labbhā. Yaṃ taṃ jātaṃ bhūtaṃ saṅkhataṃ palokadhammaṃ, taṃ vata mā palujjīti—
sn47.13:6.3.eng: How could it possibly be so that what is born, created, conditioned, and liable to wear out should not wear out?

sn47.13:6.5.pli: Seyyathāpi, ānanda, mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato yo mahantataro khandho so palujjeyya;
sn47.13:6.5.eng: Suppose there was a large tree standing with heartwood, and the largest branch broke off.
sn47.13:6.5.comm: “Wear out” and “broke off” are both palujjati.

sn47.13:6.6.pli: evameva kho ānanda, mahato bhikkhusaṅghassa tiṭṭhato sāravato sāriputto parinibbuto.
sn47.13:6.6.eng: In the same way, in the great Saṅgha that stands with heartwood, Sāriputta has become fully quenched.

sn47.13:6.7.pli: Taṃ kutettha, ānanda, labbhā. Yaṃ taṃ jātaṃ bhūtaṃ saṅkhataṃ palokadhammaṃ, taṃ vata mā palujjī’ti—
sn47.13:6.7.eng: How could it possibly be so that what is born, created, conditioned, and liable to wear out should not wear out?

sn47.13:6.9.pli: Tasmātihānanda, attadīpā viharatha attasaraṇā anaññasaraṇā, dhammadīpā dhammasaraṇā anaññasaraṇā.
sn47.13:6.9.eng: So Ānanda, live as your own island, your own refuge, with no other refuge. Let the teaching be your island and your refuge, with no other refuge.

sn47.13:7.1.pli: Kathañcānanda, bhikkhu attadīpo viharati attasaraṇo anaññasaraṇo, dhammadīpo dhammasaraṇo anaññasaraṇo?
sn47.13:7.1.eng: And how does a mendicant do this?

sn47.13:7.2.pli: Idhānanda, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ;
sn47.13:7.2.eng: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.13:7.3.eng: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

sn47.13:7.5.pli: dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.
sn47.13:7.5.eng: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.13:7.6.pli: Evaṃ kho, ānanda, bhikkhu attadīpo viharati attasaraṇo anaññasaraṇo, dhammadīpo dhammasaraṇo anaññasaraṇo.
sn47.13:7.6.eng: That’s how a mendicant lives as their own island, their own refuge, with no other refuge. That’s how the teaching is their island and their refuge, with no other refuge.

sn47.13:7.7.pli: Ye hi keci, ānanda, etarahi vā mamaccaye vā attadīpā viharissanti attasaraṇā anaññasaraṇā, dhammadīpā dhammasaraṇā anaññasaraṇā; tamatagge mete, ānanda, bhikkhū bhavissanti ye keci sikkhākāmā”ti.
sn47.13:7.7.eng: Whether now or after I have passed, any who shall live as their own island, their own refuge, with no other refuge; with the teaching as their island and their refuge, with no other refuge—those mendicants of mine who want to train shall be among the best of the best.”

sn47.14:1.1.pli: Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vajjīsu viharati ukkacelāyaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā tīre mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ aciraparinibbutesu sāriputtamoggallānesu.
sn47.14:1.1.eng: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Vajjis near Ukkacelā on the bank of the Ganges river, together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants. It was not long after Sāriputta and Moggallāna had become fully quenched.
sn47.14:1.1.comm: This must have taken place during the Buddha’s final journey depicted in the Mahāparinibbānasutta, immediately after crossing the Ganges at Pāṭaligāma (DN 16:2.1.1). It is, however, not mentioned there. Moggallāna’s death is not depicted in any early texts, as a result of which it became elaborated in a popular legend of later times.

sn47.14:1.2.pli: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto ajjhokāse nisinno hoti.
sn47.14:1.2.eng: Now, at that time the Buddha was sitting in the open, surrounded by the Saṅgha of mendicants.

sn47.14:2.1.pli: Atha kho bhagavā tuṇhībhūtaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ anuviloketvā bhikkhū āmantesi:
sn47.14:2.1.eng: Then the Buddha looked around the Saṅgha of mendicants, who were silent. He addressed them:

sn47.14:2.2.pli: “api myāyaṃ, bhikkhave, parisā suññā viya khāyati parinibbutesu sāriputtamoggallānesu.
sn47.14:2.2.eng: “Mendicants, this assembly seems empty to me now that Sāriputta and Moggallāna have become fully quenched.

sn47.14:2.3.pli: Asuññā me, bhikkhave, parisā hoti, anapekkhā tassaṃ disāyaṃ hoti, yassaṃ disāyaṃ sāriputtamoggallānā viharanti.
sn47.14:2.3.eng: My assembly never used to be empty; I had no concern for any region where Sāriputta and Moggallāna stayed.
sn47.14:2.3.comm: The text uses the same present tense as the previous sentence, but it must refer to the past. Bodhi discusses variants here.

sn47.14:2.4.pli: Ye hi te, bhikkhave, ahesuṃ atītamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā, tesampi bhagavantānaṃ etapparamaṃyeva sāvakayugaṃ ahosi—
sn47.14:2.4.eng: The Buddhas of the past or the future have pairs of chief disciples who at best were like

sn47.14:2.5.eng: Sāriputta and Moggallāna were to me.

sn47.14:2.6.pli: Yepi te, bhikkhave, bhavissanti anāgatamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā, tesampi bhagavantānaṃ etapparamaṃyeva sāvakayugaṃ bhavissati—seyyathāpi mayhaṃ sāriputtamoggallānā.

sn47.14:2.7.pli: Acchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, sāvakānaṃ, abbhutaṃ, bhikkhave, sāvakānaṃ.
sn47.14:2.7.eng: It’s an incredible and amazing quality of such disciples

sn47.14:2.8.pli: Satthu ca nāma sāsanakarā bhavissanti ovādappaṭikarā, catunnañca parisānaṃ piyā bhavissanti manāpā garubhāvanīyā ca.
sn47.14:2.8.eng: that they fulfill the Teacher’s instructions and follow his advice. And they’re liked and approved, respected and admired by the four assemblies.
sn47.14:2.8.comm: Garubhāvanīyā is a dvanda compound, “respected and admired” (see AN 5.81:1.1). | The four assemblies are monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. The number four indicates inclusivity.

sn47.14:2.9.pli: Acchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgatassa, abbhutaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgatassa.
sn47.14:2.9.eng: And it’s an incredible and amazing quality of the Realized One

sn47.14:2.10.pli: Evarūpepi nāma sāvakayuge parinibbute natthi tathāgatassa soko vā paridevo vā.
sn47.14:2.10.eng: that when such a pair of disciples becomes fully quenched he does not sorrow or lament.

sn47.14:2.11.pli: Taṃ kutettha, bhikkhave, labbhā. Yaṃ taṃ jātaṃ bhūtaṃ saṅkhataṃ palokadhammaṃ, taṃ vata mā palujjīti—
sn47.14:2.11.eng: How could it possibly be so that what is born, created, conditioned, and liable to wear out should not wear out?

sn47.14:2.13.pli: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato sāravato ye mahantatarā khandhā te palujjeyyuṃ;
sn47.14:2.13.eng: Suppose there was a large tree standing with heartwood, and the largest branches broke off.

sn47.14:2.14.pli: evameva kho, bhikkhave, mahato bhikkhusaṅghassa tiṭṭhato sāravato sāriputtamoggallānā parinibbutā.
sn47.14:2.14.eng: In the same way, in the great Saṅgha that stands with heartwood, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have become fully quenched.

sn47.14:2.15.pli: Taṃ kutettha, bhikkhave, labbhā. Yaṃ taṃ jātaṃ bhūtaṃ saṅkhataṃ palokadhammaṃ, taṃ vata mā palujjīti—
sn47.14:2.15.eng: How could it possibly be so that what is born, created, conditioned, and liable to wear out should not wear out?

sn47.14:2.17.pli: Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, attadīpā viharatha attasaraṇā anaññasaraṇā, dhammadīpā dhammasaraṇā anaññasaraṇā.
sn47.14:2.17.eng: So mendicants, live as your own island, your own refuge, with no other refuge. Let the teaching be your island and your refuge, with no other refuge.

sn47.14:3.1.pli: Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu attadīpo viharati attasaraṇo anaññasaraṇo, dhammadīpo dhammasaraṇo anaññasaraṇo?
sn47.14:3.1.eng: And how does a mendicant do this?

sn47.14:3.2.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ;
sn47.14:3.2.eng: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.14:3.3.eng: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

sn47.14:3.5.pli: dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.
sn47.14:3.5.eng: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.14:3.6.pli: Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu attadīpo viharati attasaraṇo anaññasaraṇo, dhammadīpo dhammasaraṇo anaññasaraṇo.
sn47.14:3.6.eng: That’s how a mendicant lives as their own island, their own refuge, with no other refuge. That’s how the teaching is their island and their refuge, with no other refuge.

sn47.14:3.7.pli: Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, etarahi vā mamaccaye vā attadīpā viharissanti attasaraṇā anaññasaraṇā, dhammadīpā dhammasaraṇā anaññasaraṇā; tamatagge mete, bhikkhave, bhikkhū bhavissanti ye keci sikkhākāmā”ti.
sn47.14:3.7.eng: Whether now or after I have passed, any who shall live as their own island, their own refuge, with no other refuge; with the teaching as their island and their refuge, with no other refuge—those mendicants of mine who want to train shall be among the best of the best.”

sn47.15:1.2.pli: Atha kho āyasmā bāhiyo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā bāhiyo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca:
sn47.15:1.2.eng: Then Venerable Bāhiya went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:
sn47.15:1.2.comm: For this Bāhiya, see note on SN 35.89:1.1.

sn47.15:1.3.pli: “sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṃ desetu, yamahaṃ bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto vihareyyan”ti.
sn47.15:1.3.eng: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

sn47.15:1.4.pli: “Tasmātiha tvaṃ, bāhiya, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu.
sn47.15:1.4.eng: “Well then, Bāhiya, you should purify the starting point of skillful qualities.

sn47.15:1.5.eng: What is the starting point of skillful qualities?

sn47.15:1.6.eng: Well purified ethics and correct view.

sn47.15:1.7.pli: Yato ca kho te, bāhiya, sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ bhavissati, diṭṭhi ca ujukā, tato tvaṃ, bāhiya, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāveyyāsi.
sn47.15:1.7.eng: When your ethics are well purified and your view is correct, you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, depending on and grounded on ethics.

sn47.15:2.2.pli: Idha tvaṃ, bāhiya, kāye kāyānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ;
sn47.15:2.2.eng: Meditate observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.15:2.3.eng: Meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

sn47.15:2.5.pli: dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.
sn47.15:2.5.eng: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.15:2.6.pli: Yato kho tvaṃ, bāhiya, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāvessasi, tato tuyhaṃ, bāhiya, yā ratti vā divaso vā āgamissati, vuddhiyeva pāṭikaṅkhā kusalesu dhammesu, no parihānī”ti.
sn47.15:2.6.eng: When you develop these four kinds of mindfulness meditation, depending on and grounded on ethics, you can expect growth, not decline, in skillful qualities, whether by day or by night.”

sn47.15:3.1.pli: Atha kho āyasmā bāhiyo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi.
sn47.15:3.1.eng: And then Venerable Bāhiya approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

sn47.15:3.2.pli: Atha kho āyasmā bāhiyo eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto viharanto nacirasseva—yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti, tadanuttaraṃ—brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsi.
sn47.15:3.2.eng: Then Bāhiya, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme end of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

sn47.15:3.3.pli: “Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā”ti abbhaññāsi.
sn47.15:3.3.eng: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

sn47.15:3.4.pli: Aññataro ca panāyasmā bāhiyo arahataṃ ahosīti.
sn47.15:3.4.eng: And Venerable Bāhiya became one of the perfected.

sn47.16:1.2.pli: Atha kho āyasmā uttiyo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami …pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā uttiyo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca:
sn47.16:1.2.eng: Then Venerable Uttiya went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

sn47.16:1.3.pli: “sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṃ desetu, yamahaṃ bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto vihareyyan”ti.
sn47.16:1.3.eng: “Sir, may the Buddha please teach me Dhamma in brief. When I’ve heard it, I’ll live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.”

sn47.16:1.4.pli: “Tasmātiha tvaṃ, uttiya, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu.
sn47.16:1.4.eng: “Well then, Uttiya, you should purify the starting point of skillful qualities.

sn47.16:1.5.eng: What is the starting point of skillful qualities?

sn47.16:1.6.eng: Well purified ethics and correct view.

sn47.16:1.7.pli: Yato ca kho te, uttiya, sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ bhavissati, diṭṭhi ca ujukā, tato tvaṃ, uttiya, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāveyyāsi.
sn47.16:1.7.eng: When your ethics are well purified and your view is correct, you should develop the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, depending on and grounded on ethics.

sn47.16:2.2.pli: Idha tvaṃ, uttiya, kāye kāyānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ;
sn47.16:2.2.eng: Meditate observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.16:2.3.eng: Meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

sn47.16:2.5.pli: dhammesu dhammānupassī viharāhi ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.
sn47.16:2.5.eng: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.16:2.6.pli: Yato kho tvaṃ, uttiya, sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāvessasi, tato tvaṃ, uttiya, gamissasi maccudheyyassa pāran”ti.
sn47.16:2.6.eng: When you develop these four kinds of mindfulness meditation, depending on and grounded on ethics, you’ll cross beyond Death’s dominion.”

sn47.16:3.1.pli: Atha kho āyasmā uttiyo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi.
sn47.16:3.1.eng: And then Venerable Uttiya approved and agreed with what the Buddha said. He got up from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

sn47.16:3.2.pli: Atha kho āyasmā uttiyo eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto viharanto nacirasseva—yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti, tadanuttaraṃ—brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsi.
sn47.16:3.2.eng: Then Uttiya, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme end of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.

sn47.16:3.3.pli: “Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā”ti abbhaññāsi.
sn47.16:3.3.eng: He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.”

sn47.16:3.4.pli: Aññataro ca panāyasmā uttiyo arahataṃ ahosīti.
sn47.16:3.4.eng: And Venerable Uttiya became one of the perfected.

sn47.17:1.1.pli: “Cattārome, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ariyā niyyānikā niyyanti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya.
sn47.17:1.1.eng: “Mendicants, when these four kinds of mindfulness meditation are developed and cultivated they are noble and emancipating, and bring one who practices them to the complete ending of suffering.

sn47.17:1.3.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ;
sn47.17:1.3.eng: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.17:1.4.eng: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

sn47.17:1.6.pli: dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.
sn47.17:1.6.eng: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.17:1.7.pli: Ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ariyā niyyānikā niyyanti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyā”ti.
sn47.17:1.7.eng: When these four kinds of mindfulness meditation are developed and cultivated they are noble and emancipating, and bring one who practices them to the complete ending of suffering.”

sn47.18:1.1.pli: Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā uruvelāyaṃ viharati najjā nerañjarāya tīre ajapālanigrodhe paṭhamābhisambuddho.
sn47.18:1.1.eng: At one time, when he was first awakened, the Buddha was staying in Uruvelā at the goatherd’s banyan tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.
sn47.18:1.1.comm: This discourse is a good example of how the Satipaṭṭhānasutta (MN 10, DN 22) was constructed. The famous opening phrase is found here, where it is associated with Brahmā. It turns out that ekāyana is in fact a term found prominently in Brahmanical texts, used in the context of renunciation and contemplation to mean “convergence”, just as in Pali. In the Satipaṭṭhānasutta this connection is lost, as there is no Brahmanical context. Commentators subsequently struggled to explain the word, offering a range of possibilities, to which ancient Chinese translators and modern authors added more. The current sutta allows us to restore the Brahmanical context and determine the correct meaning. This further suggests that this is the original context, where the word had a contextual meaning, and it was later excerpted for the opening of the Satipaṭṭhānasutta. | This same discourse is presented as a first-person recollection of the Buddha at SN 47.43.

sn47.18:1.2.pli: Atha kho bhagavato rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi:
sn47.18:1.2.eng: Then as he was in private retreat this thought came to his mind,

sn47.18:1.3.pli: “ekāyanvāyaṃ maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ—cattāro satipaṭṭhānā.
sn47.18:1.3.eng: “The four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the path to convergence. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.
sn47.18:1.3.comm: The phrase ekāyano maggo (“path to convergence”) is used in only one other context in Pali, where it means to “come together with” (MN 12:37.5). Here the Buddha’s phrase is echoed by Brahmā, which suggests it was a Brahmanical term. Yajñavalkya—in a core passage full of details shared with the suttas—uses it for a place where things unite or converge (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.11; in the same sense also at Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.5.2; Mahābhārata 14.19.1–2). Thus satipaṭṭhāna leads to everything “coming together as one”. In other words, as seventh factor of the noble eightfold path, it leads to samādhi, the eighth factor (SN 45.1:3.9; see also MN 44:12.3). Ekāyana is also a name for a certain Sanskrit scripture (in a list of texts at Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.2, 7.1.4, 7.2.1, 7.7.1; Puruṣottamasaṁhitā 1.10; Praśnasaṁhitā 2.38). Now, the latter text discusses the ekāyana as nivṛtti, “renunciation”, which is, in fact, introduced to the Vedic system by Yajñavalkya in the above-cited passage. Thus as a scripture it probably originally referred to that very passage exemplifying the Upaniṣadic teachings, which are otherwise omitted from the Chāndogya list.

sn47.18:2.2.pli: Kāye vā bhikkhu kāyānupassī vihareyya ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ;
sn47.18:2.2.eng: A mendicant would meditate observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.
sn47.18:2.2.comm: This is phrased in optative because the Buddha is contemplating what would happen were he to teach and start his dispensation. Similarly, idha (“here”) is absent since it is not a present situation.

sn47.18:2.3.eng: Or they’d meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

sn47.18:2.5.pli: dhammesu vā bhikkhu dhammānupassī vihareyya ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.
sn47.18:2.5.eng: or principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.18:2.6.pli: Ekāyanvāyaṃ maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ—cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti.
sn47.18:2.6.eng: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the path to convergence. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.”

sn47.18:3.1.pli: Atha kho brahmā sahampati bhagavato cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya—seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya; evameva kho brahmaloke antarahito bhagavato purato pāturahosi.
sn47.18:3.1.eng: Then the divinity Sahampati knew the Buddha’s train of thought. As easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, he vanished from the realm of divinity and reappeared in front of the Buddha.
sn47.18:3.1.comm: Sahampati’s appearance here underscores the centrality of mindfulness and acts as a divine endoresemnt (see SN 6.1:5.1 and note).

sn47.18:3.2.pli: Atha kho brahmā sahampati ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca:
sn47.18:3.2.eng: He arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his joined palms toward the Buddha, and said:

sn47.18:3.3.eng: “That’s so true, Blessed One! That’s so true, Holy One!

sn47.18:3.4.pli: Ekāyanvāyaṃ, bhante, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ—cattāro satipaṭṭhānā.
sn47.18:3.4.eng: Sir, the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the path to convergence. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.

sn47.18:4.2.pli: Kāye vā, bhante, bhikkhu kāyānupassī vihareyya ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ;
sn47.18:4.2.eng: A mendicant would meditate observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.18:4.3.eng: Or they’d meditate observing an aspect of feelings …

sn47.18:4.5.pli: dhammesu vā, bhante, bhikkhu dhammānupassī vihareyya ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.
sn47.18:4.5.eng: or principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

sn47.18:4.6.pli: Ekāyanvāyaṃ, bhante, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ—cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti.
sn47.18:4.6.eng: The four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the path to convergence. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.”

sn47.18:5.1.eng: That’s what the divinity Sahampati said.

sn47.18:5.2.eng: Then he went on to say:

sn47.18:6.1.eng: “The compassionate one, <j>who sees the ending of rebirth,

sn47.18:6.3.eng: By this path people crossed over before,

sn47.19:1.1.pli: Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sumbhesu viharati sedakaṃ nāma sumbhānaṃ nigamo.
sn47.19:1.1.eng: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sumbhas, near the town of the Sumbhas named Sedaka.
sn47.19:1.1.comm: This may be modern Sambalpur in Odisha, near the bay of Bengal on India’s east coast. This Sutta is the earliest description of Indian pole acrobatics or mallakambha. Further east lies Chandraketugarh in West Bengal, where the earliest physical evidence for mallakambha has been found. One pot from around 200 BCE shows, in detailed and graceful style, three acrobats using a T-shaped pole. One man kneels, holding the pole in his hands with great strength and balance, while a man and a woman perform acrobatics on opposite bars of the T. A crowd of women and men look on in amazement.

sn47.19:1.2.eng: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:

sn47.19:1.3.pli: “bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, caṇḍālavaṃsiko caṇḍālavaṃsaṃ ussāpetvā medakathālikaṃ antevāsiṃ āmantesi:
sn47.19:1.3.eng: “Once upon a time, mendicants, a pole acrobat of the corpse-workers set up the bamboo pole of his tribe and said to his apprentice Medakathālikā,
sn47.19:1.3.comm: While the terms are not easy to interpret, it appears that it was a practice of the “corpse-workers” (caṇḍāla), the most despised caste (see SN 3.21:2.2 and note). Perhaps it originated as a tribal ritual or sport. Further references to this practice are found in DN 1:1.13.2 (see note there) and Ja 498, which is set near the opposite coast in Ujjeni.

sn47.19:1.4.pli: ‘ehi tvaṃ, samma medakathālike, caṇḍālavaṃsaṃ abhiruhitvā mama uparikhandhe tiṭṭhāhī’ti.
sn47.19:1.4.eng: ‘Come now, dear Medakathālikā, climb up the bamboo pole and stand above my shoulders.’
sn47.19:1.4.comm: Medakathālikā (“frying pan”) was a woman, which agrees with the depiction on the Chandraketugarh pottery.

sn47.19:1.5.pli: ‘Evaṃ, ācariyā’ti kho, bhikkhave, medakathālikā antevāsī caṇḍālavaṃsikassa paṭissutvā caṇḍālavaṃsaṃ abhiruhitvā ācariyassa uparikhandhe aṭṭhāsi.
sn47.19:1.5.eng: ‘Yes, tutor,’ she replied. She climbed up the bamboo pole and stood above her tutor’s shoulders.

sn47.19:1.6.pli: Atha kho, bhikkhave, caṇḍālavaṃsiko medakathālikaṃ antevāsiṃ etadavoca:
sn47.19:1.6.eng: Then the pole acrobat of the corpse-workers said to Medakathālikā,

sn47.19:1.7.pli: ‘tvaṃ, samma medakathālike, mamaṃ rakkha, ahaṃ taṃ rakkhissāmi.
sn47.19:1.7.eng: ‘You look after me, dear Medakathālikā, and I shall look after you.

sn47.19:1.8.pli: Evaṃ mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ guttā aññamaññaṃ rakkhitā sippāni ceva dassessāma, lābhañca lacchāma, sotthinā ca caṇḍālavaṃsā orohissāmā’ti.
sn47.19:1.8.eng: That’s how, guarding and looking after each other, we’ll display our skill, collect our fee, and get down safely from the bamboo pole.’
sn47.19:1.8.comm: The text implies that both acrobats were up the pole. Perhaps the plural is just a figure of speech, but in the pottery depiction there are indeed two suspended acrobats. I think the pole is planted on the ground, with the master half-way up, and Medakathālikā above him.

sn47.19:1.9.pli: Evaṃ vutte, bhikkhave, medakathālikā antevāsī caṇḍālavaṃsikaṃ etadavoca:
sn47.19:1.9.eng: When he said this, Medakathālikā said to her teacher,

sn47.19:1.10.eng: ‘That’s not how it will be, tutor!

sn47.19:1.11.pli: Tvaṃ, ācariya, attānaṃ rakkha, ahaṃ attānaṃ rakkhissāmi.
sn47.19:1.11.eng: You look after yourself, and I shall look after myself.

sn47.19:1.12.pli: Evaṃ mayaṃ attaguttā attarakkhitā sippāni ceva dassessāma, lābhañca lacchāma, sotthinā ca caṇḍālavaṃsā orohissāmā’”ti.
sn47.19:1.12.eng: That’s how, guarding and looking after ourselves, we’ll display our skill, collect our fee, and get down safely from the bamboo pole.’

sn47.19:2.1.pli: “So tattha ñāyo”ti bhagavā etadavoca, “yathā medakathālikā antevāsī ācariyaṃ avoca.
sn47.19:2.1.eng: That’s the way,” said the Buddha. “It’s just as Medakathālikā said to her tutor.
sn47.19:2.1.comm: The text is a little unclear, but it seems that Medakathālikā was pointing out that by looking after oneself we are also looking after the other. It is remarkable how the Buddha is adopting the wisdom of a woman from such a despised caste.

sn47.19:2.2.eng: Thinking ‘I’ll look after myself,’ you should cultivate mindfulness meditation.

sn47.19:2.3.eng: Thinking ‘I’ll look after others,’ you should cultivate mindfulness meditation.

sn47.19:2.4.pli: Attānaṃ, bhikkhave, rakkhanto paraṃ rakkhati, paraṃ rakkhanto attānaṃ rakkhati.
sn47.19:2.4.eng: Looking after yourself, you look after others; and looking after others, you look after yourself.

sn47.19:3.1.pli: Kathañca, bhikkhave, attānaṃ rakkhanto paraṃ rakkhati?
sn47.19:3.1.eng: And how do you look after others by looking after yourself?

sn47.19:3.2.eng: By development, cultivation, and practice of meditation.

sn47.19:3.3.pli: evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, attānaṃ rakkhanto paraṃ rakkhati.

sn47.19:3.4.pli: Kathañca, bhikkhave, paraṃ rakkhanto attānaṃ rakkhati?
sn47.19:3.4.eng: And how do you look after yourself by looking after others?

sn47.19:3.5.eng: By acceptance, harmlessness, love, and sympathy.

sn47.19:3.6.pli: evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, paraṃ rakkhanto attānaṃ rakkhati.

sn47.19:3.7.eng: Thinking ‘I’ll look after myself,’ you should cultivate mindfulness meditation.

sn47.19:3.8.eng: Thinking ‘I’ll look after others,’ you should cultivate mindfulness meditation.

sn47.19:3.9.pli: Attānaṃ, bhikkhave, rakkhanto paraṃ rakkhati, paraṃ rakkhanto attānaṃ rakkhatī”ti.
sn47.19:3.9.eng: Looking after yourself, you look after others; and looking after others, you look after yourself.”
